title: Bhakti yoga: the nine forms of devotion; the Alvars and Nayanars; Mirabai, Tulsidas, Surdas; kirtan as method (2 of 7)
hook: nine ways to love God, and a famous name standing beside each one
tomorrow: Bhakti yoga: the nine forms of devotion; the Alvars and Nayanars; Mirabai, Tulsidas, Surdas; kirtan as method (3 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti yoga. A leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water. And Prahlada in his father's lap, listing nine ways to love. Today, all nine.
screen: `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.`

segments.voice: People love differently. Some say it. Some show it with food. Some just show up, every time, and never say a word. Some love by listening, really listening. In plenty of families the love is all there; it just comes in different shapes. Prahlada's list is the bhakti tradition noticing the same thing about loving God. It's not one feeling. It's nine doors into the same room, and tradition even gives each door a famous person who walked through it.
screen: `PEOPLE LOVE DIFFERENTLY.` → `SAY IT, SHOW IT, SHOW UP.` → `NINE DOORS, ONE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in the order Prahlada gives them in the Bhagavata Purana. One: shravana, hearing the stories of God. Tradition's example is King Parikshit, who heard the whole Bhagavata before he died. Two: kirtana, singing praise aloud: the sage Shuka, who told Parikshit those stories. Three: smarana, remembering, keeping God in mind: Prahlada himself. Four: pada-sevana, serving the feet, humble, close service: the goddess Lakshmi, at Vishnu's feet. Five: archana, worship with offerings, lamp and flower and water: King Prithu. Six: vandana, bowing and praising: Akrura, who bowed to the ground when he met Krishna. Seven: dasya, being a servant: Hanuman, who wanted nothing but to serve Rama. Eight: sakhya, friendship: Arjuna, whose chariot Krishna drove into battle, as a friend. Nine: atma-nivedana, giving your whole self: King Bali, who gave everything he had, even his own head to be stepped on. Notice how the list moves: the ear, then the voice, then the mind. Then the hands, then the whole body bowing. Then relationships, servant, then friend. And it ends with a person handing over themselves. It's a ladder, and it's also a menu. Some teachers say a person may find one or two doors that fit and live there for years. A grandmother who can't sit through a sermon but sings every evening. A quiet man who never sings but sweeps the temple steps. Same room.
screen: `THE EAR, THE VOICE, THE MIND.` · `THE HANDS AND THE BOWED HEAD.` · `SERVANT, THEN FRIEND.` · `GIVING YOUR WHOLE SELF.` · then, large: `LOVE AS THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly past the nine doors: hearing, singing, remembering, serving at the feet, offering, bowing, being a servant, friendship, giving yourself. Notice which one feels like home, not the one you think is best, and stay with it. If you pray, walk through that door now, quietly; if you don't, just notice which shape your love usually takes, with anyone.
Bhakti yoga. The nine forms of devotion, navadha bhakti: hearing, singing, remembering, serving, worship, bowing, servanthood, friendship and giving yourself.
Your line: love as the road. Nine doors open into one room. Until tomorrow, then.

howItsDone: Hindu devotional teachers often present the nine forms of bhakti from the Bhagavata Purana as a range of practices, from listening to sacred stories and singing to service and complete self-offering, and devotees tend to settle into the forms that suit them.

original.note: Sanskrit: navadhā bhakti, devotion in nine forms (nava, nine), as listed in the Bhagavata Purana 7.5.23–24.

trapdoor: what you thought: devotion is a single feeling.
what it means: bhakti has nine recognized forms, from hearing to giving your whole self.

what a scholar hears: the list is Bhagavata Purana 7.5.23–24; the pairing of each form with an exemplar (Parikshit, Shuka, Prahlada, Lakshmi, Prithu, Akrura, Hanuman, Arjuna, Bali) comes from a later devotional verse cited by Gaudiya and other Vaishnava teachers.
